name: Northern Gulf of Mexico
blurb: Where the river ends: shrimp, menhaden, dolphins and the summer dead zone.

tip.title: Cut the oxygen
tip.text: Each summer, bacteria feeding on dead algae use up the oxygen near the sea floor. Cut Bottom-water oxygen by 80% and see which bottom dwellers suffer.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gulf of Mexico dead zone

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. The what-if model can show the effect of less oxygen, but it cannot show the algal blooms that cause it. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Tiny grazers of phytoplankton. Adult menhaden and bay anchovies eat them.
A small schooling fish that eats zooplankton. Wikipedia notes anchovies may temporarily increase in hypoxic water.
Filters algae from the water. Wikipedia notes oysters face more disease under hypoxia.
An omnivore that eats oysters, worms and carrion.
A jellyfish. Wikipedia says jellyfish can survive hypoxia and may increase when competitors and predators leave.

nodes.name: Bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: Eats fish, shrimp and squid, often herding schools toward shore. Large sharks including bull sharks prey on it.
Warm, bright surface water lets blooms grow fast in summer.
Warm, layered water traps oxygen-poor water near the bottom. Bottom dwellers that cannot leave suffocate when oxygen falls very low.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae. In summer this uses up bottom-water oxygen and creates the dead zone.

story: Gulf Islands National Seashore preserves natural and historic resources along the Gulf of Mexico barrier islands of Florida, Alabama, and Mississippi. The protected regions include mainland areas and parts of seven islands. The barrier islands started forming 4500 to 5400 years ago.
matters: The seashore includes the 4,080 acres Gulf Islands Wilderness, offering special protection to parts of Petit Bois Island and Horn Island in Mississippi.
